(a) **Short notes:**
* **(i) Allenes:** Allenes are organic compounds containing adjacent (cumulated) double bonds, represented as $\text{R}_2\text{C}=\text{C}=\text{CR}_2$. Substituted allenes exhibit axial chirality and can show optical isomerism even in the absence of a chiral carbon center because their terminal groups lie in perpendicular planes.
* **(ii) Spiranes:** Spiranes (or spiro compounds) are bicyclic organic molecules sharing a single common carbon atom (the spiro atom) between two rings. The rings are oriented in perpendicular planes, which can impart optical activity (chirality) if the substituents are suitably unsymmetrical.

(b) **Decreasing order of acidic strength:**
Looking at the given nitro-substituted benzoic acid derivatives (assuming standard positions (i) ortho-nitrobenzoic acid, (ii) meta-nitrobenzoic acid, (iii) para-nitrobenzoic acid):
* **Order:** $\text{(i)} > \text{(iii)} > \text{(ii)}$
* **Reason:** Ortho-substituted benzoic acids experience the *ortho-effect*, making them exceptionally strong acids due to steric inhibition of resonance and local field effects. Para-nitrobenzoic acid is more acidic than meta-nitrobenzoic acid because the $-\text{NO}_2$ group exerts a strong $-M$ (mesomeric) effect from the para position, whereas from the meta position, it operates exclusively via the weaker $-I$ (inductive) effect.

(c) **Stability of Singlet vs Triplet Carbene:**
* **Triplet carbene** is **more stable** than singlet carbene in the gas phase.
* **Reason:** In triplet carbene, the two non-bonding electrons occupy two different degenerate $sp^2$ orbitals with parallel spins (Hund's rule), minimizing electronic repulsion and spatial crowding. In contrast, singlet carbene has both electrons paired in the same orbital, resulting in higher electron-electron repulsion and higher energy.

(d) **Suzuki-Miyayura Cross-Coupling Reaction:**
The Suzuki coupling is the palladium-catalyzed cross-coupling reaction between an organoboron compound ($\text{R}-\text{B}(\text{OH})_2$) and an organic halide ($\text{R}'-\text{X}$) in the presence of a base to form a new carbon-carbon bond ($\text{R}-\text{R}'$).

$$\text{R}-\text{B}(\text{OH})_2 + \text{R}'-\text{X} \xrightarrow[\text{Base}]{\text{Pd Catalyst}} \text{R}-\text{R}' + \text{HX-Basecomplex}$$

* **Mechanism Steps:**
  1. **Oxidative Addition:** $\text{Pd}(0)$ catalyst inserts into the carbon-halide bond of the organic halide to form an organopalladium(II) complex.
  2. **Transmetalation:** The base activates the boronic acid, allowing transfer of the organic group from boron to the palladium complex, replacing the halide.
  3. **Reductive Elimination:** The two coupled organic groups eliminate from the palladium center, forming the bi-product $\text{R}-\text{R}'$ and regenerating the active $\text{Pd}(0)$ catalyst.
